courseMetadata.title: Data Modeling & API Design: Shape at Rest, on the Wire, at the Edge
courseMetadata.description: An intermediate course for senior developers who already ship features but make storage and API decisions by habit. You will work one decision chain end to end: **the shape you choose at rest constrains the contract you can offer, and the contract constrains what the frontend can do without waterfalls or heroics.**

prerequisites.description: Comfortable writing SQL `SELECT` statements with joins, and reading a query plan at a glance.
Have shipped and maintained at least one HTTP API that other teams consumed.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: The three core experiences are one decision chain. Injecting retrieval across them forces learners to re-evaluate a storage choice from the contract's point of view, and a contract from the frontend's.
Cost-of-change items (evolution, pagination depth, amplification) interleave well because they share one underlying question: who pays, and when.

probeQuestions.prompt: A tracking endpoint answers "where is parcel X" by selecting the newest row from a 4-billion-row `scan` table. You add an index on `(parcel_id, scanned_at DESC)` and p99 drops from 400ms to 12ms. Traffic then triples and p99 returns to 180ms. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: The index reduced selection cost but the request still visits a second table; that per-request work scales with request volume.
The index is the complete fix; the real problem is hardware, so scale the read replicas.
The planner has stopped choosing the index; refresh statistics and add a query hint.
The table should move to a document store, where this lookup is inherently faster.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. An index changes the cost of *finding* rows; it does not remove the fact that the answer lives in a second table and is recomputed per request.
No amount of hardware removes work the shape makes mandatory — and the symptom scaling with traffic is the tell.
A plan regression appears suddenly, not in proportion to request volume; this symptom points at per-request work instead.
The speedup people attribute to document stores comes from co-locating related data, which you can do relationally with a summary column and no engine change.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: What does an index change, and what does it leave untouched?

probeQuestions.prompt: Team A runs a single-node document database. Team B runs a relational primary with three asynchronous read replicas and routes all reads to the replicas. Which statement is true?
options: Team A's reads are strongly consistent; Team B's are not.
Team B's reads are strongly consistent because the engine is relational and supports ACID transactions.
Team A's reads are eventually consistent because document stores trade consistency for availability.
Both are strongly consistent, since neither is running across multiple regions.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Consistency follows topology and configuration: a single node serves its own latest writes; an asynchronous replica may not.
ACID describes what happens inside a transaction on the primary and says nothing about what a replica has received yet.
That tradeoff belongs to replicated, partitioned deployments — a single node has no replication lag to trade away.
Replication lag does not require multiple regions; a replica in the same rack can still be behind.

probeQuestions.prompt: An existing response field `station.name` has always been non-nullable. Which change to it is breaking for consumers, and why?
options: Making it nullable — consumers dereferenced it without a null branch.
Making it non-nullable when it was nullable — consumers will now receive unexpected values.
Neither; nullability is metadata and does not affect running clients.
Both directions equally; any change to a published field is breaking.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct, and this asymmetry is the whole rule: you can always tighten a contract, never loosen it.
Backwards. Tightening leaves the consumer's existing null branch as dead code, which is harmless.
Nullability is the single hardest property to change post-release, because typed clients encode it directly into their code paths.
Treating change itself as the risk hides the direction that matters and leads teams to version everything.

probeQuestions.prompt: A listener loads page 1 of a comment feed with `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0`, a new comment arrives, and they tap next page (`OFFSET 20`). They see a comment they already read. What is the cause?
options: `OFFSET` names a position in a freshly computed result set, and the insert shifted every row one position later.
The index on the sort column is missing, so row order is nondeterministic between queries.
The client cached page 1 and re-rendered it; the server returned the correct rows.
The page size is too large; smaller pages reduce the chance of overlap.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — and note this is a correctness defect, not a performance one. Infinite hardware would not fix it.
An index fixes ordering determinism and per-row cost, but this duplicate occurs with a perfect index in place.
A client-side re-render would show the duplicate immediately, not on the next fetch; the server genuinely returned the row twice.
Smaller pages change how often you notice, not whether it happens — the shift is one row per insert regardless of page size.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: Why does OFFSET pagination return duplicates when rows are inserted between page fetches?

probeQuestions.prompt: Fifty episodes each need their host name, currently fetched one query per episode. A colleague wraps the fifty calls in `Promise.all` and the page gets much faster. In two or three sentences: what has been fixed, what has not, and what new failure mode has been introduced?
scoringCriteria: Names that latency improved because the calls now overlap.
States that the query *count* is unchanged — fifty queries still leave the service.
Identifies the new failure mode: fifty concurrent connections, so pool exhaustion replaces slowness and can take down unrelated endpoints.

probeQuestions.prompt: You run a public API with eleven third-party consumers whose query patterns you cannot predict, very high read volume on a handful of shapes, and heavy CDN caching. A team proposes replacing it with GraphQL. What is the strongest objection?
options: You lose URL-keyed HTTP caching and take on an obligation to bound query cost from untrusted clients.
There is no real objection — GraphQL is a superset of REST, so this is a straightforward upgrade.
GraphQL pushes query planning to the client, so server cost becomes less predictable to monitor but cheaper overall.
GraphQL tooling is less mature, so third-party developers will struggle to integrate.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The two things this audience depends on most are exactly the two GraphQL turns from defaults into projects.
They optimize different things; treating one as a generational successor hides the caching and cost-bounding you would be giving up.
The reverse: arbitrary client queries make depth limiting, cost analysis and persisted queries mandatory server-side work.
A weak and dated objection about ecosystem rather than about this audience's traffic and trust profile.

competencies.title: Selecting a storage model against workload characteristics
competencies.description: Evaluate relational vs. document (and hybrid) storage for a given read/write mix, access-pattern set, and consistency requirement, and justify the choice in terms of cost of change rather than cost of query.

desiredOutcomes.description: Given a workload profile, choose a storage model and defend it against the two strongest counterarguments.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Choice is justified by access patterns and cost of change, not by engine reputation or benchmark folklore.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Document stores are schemaless, so you don't have to model the data up front.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The schema still exists — it has simply moved out of the database and into every application that reads the data, where it is unenforced and unversioned. Choosing a document model is incomplete until you name who validates the payload and how its versions are tracked.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Return to Worked Example B and complete Step 4 explicitly: for any document design, write down the version tag, the validating reader, and the code owner. A document design without those three is an unfinished design.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: NoSQL is just faster than a relational database.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: This conflates data model with performance. Where the speedup is real, it comes from co-locating data that is accessed together — and the same co-location in a relational store (a summary column, a covering index) produces the same effect without changing engines.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the Section 1 runnable example, then ask: which part of this win came from the engine, and which came from not having to visit a second table? Only the second is transferable.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Postgres has JSONB, so the relational-versus-document choice doesn't matter any more.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: JSONB relaxes column rigidity inside a transactional engine, which is often the right answer — but it does not change transaction scope, does not give the planner useful statistics about nested values, and does not decide who validates the payload. The tradeoff moved; it did not vanish.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For any JSONB proposal, answer the three questions it does not answer: what is the transaction boundary, how will the planner estimate selectivity on nested fields, and who rejects a malformed payload?

competencies.title: Designing schema from access patterns
competencies.description: Produce a concrete schema — tables or collections, keys, indexes, denormalizations — derived from an enumerated, frequency-ranked list of queries rather than from an entity-relationship sketch.

desiredOutcomes.description: Translate a ranked list of queries into a schema with keys, indexes and justified denormalizations, naming the pattern you deliberately made slow.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Every index names the pattern it serves; every denormalized column names the transaction that maintains it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Normalize to third normal form first, then optimize later once you see real traffic.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: This treats denormalization as a repair rather than a design input. At scale the dominant read pattern determines the shape, and retrofitting it means a migration on the largest table you own — which is exactly the change teams never get budget to make.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Before drawing any table, write the access-pattern table with frequencies. If you cannot fill in the frequency column, you are not ready to design the schema.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Denormalizing means accepting that the copy will drift out of date.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: This conflates duplication with asynchrony. A duplicated value written inside the same transaction as the fact it summarizes, guarded against out-of-order writes, is never stale — it is a second physical copy of a fact that was committed once.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-do the Section 1 code challenge `apply_scan` and then read the write path in Worked Example A. If a denormalized column is stale, the bug is in the write path, not in the decision to denormalize.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a query is slow, the right fix is always an index.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Indexes accelerate selection — finding the qualifying rows. They cannot change shape: if answering a question requires visiting a second table or recomputing an aggregate per request, an index makes that work fast per row without removing it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Ask of any slow query: is the cost per row, or is it the number of structures the request must touch? Only the first is an index problem.

competencies.title: Drawing transaction and aggregate boundaries
competencies.description: Determine what must be written atomically, where that boundary should sit, and what the application must do when a required invariant spans the boundary.

desiredOutcomes.description: Place a transaction boundary around the invariants of a domain and choose a correct strategy for anything that crosses it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: States what an observer sees during any inconsistency window, rather than estimating how long the window is.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Relational databases are strongly consistent and document databases are eventually consistent.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Both properties are configuration and topology, not data model. A single-node document store is strongly consistent; a relational primary read through an asynchronous replica is not.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For any consistency claim, name the topology: how many nodes, which one is being read, and is replication synchronous? The engine's name is not part of the answer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Eventual consistency means the data is correct within a second or two.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: No bound is guaranteed. A stuck consumer or a backed-up queue means hours, not seconds. A design that is only correct when the lag is small is not a design; it is a bet.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Replace the question 'how long is the window?' with 'what does an observer see during the window, and is that acceptable at any duration?'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: I'll just wrap the two service calls in a transaction.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: There is no shared transaction manager across two services with two databases, so there is no transaction to open. The honest alternatives are collapsing the boundary, an idempotent retryable message, or compensation with reconciliation.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Work Worked Example C again and write down all three options explicitly before choosing, including the unfashionable one: putting both facts back in the same database.

competencies.title: Choosing an API paradigm
competencies.description: Evaluate REST, GraphQL and RPC-style contracts against client diversity, caching needs, team topology and operational maturity.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select a paradigm per audience and state the specific costs the choice incurs, without using the word 'better'.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names at least three of: caching, composition, cost-bounding, observability, evolution mechanism.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: GraphQL is the newer thing; it supersedes REST.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: They optimize different things. GraphQL moves composition to the client, at the cost of HTTP caching, predictable server cost, and per-endpoint observability. Mature systems frequently run both, for different audiences.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Fill in the five-row comparison table from Worked Example B for your own system. Every row should say what you pay, not which side wins.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: REST means JSON over HTTP with the right verbs.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Verb hygiene is the smallest part. The substance is resource identity (what is addressable and what the URL means), representation (what the response says about that resource) and cache semantics (what the response says about its own reusability). Perfect verbs over unaddressable, uncacheable responses buy nothing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Audit one endpoint for the three substantive properties: is the thing addressable, is the representation stable, and does the response declare its own cacheability?

commonMisconceptions.misconception: GraphQL removes the need for server-side query planning — the client decides what it wants.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It relocates planning rather than removing it. Arbitrary client queries make depth limiting, cost analysis, persisted queries and per-field instrumentation mandatory rather than optional.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Before adopting GraphQL for untrusted clients, write the depth limit, the cost budget, and the persisted-query policy. If you cannot, you are not ready to expose it.

competencies.title: Designing the API contract as its own model
competencies.description: Design resources and types, field nullability, error representation and identifiers as a deliberate model that mirrors neither the database below nor the current UI above.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a resource contract and articulate, field by field, where it deliberately diverges from storage and from the screen.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Identifiers are opaque, money carries a currency, state is a domain enum, and every nullable field is a decision with a reason.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The API should expose the tables — it's the same data, so why transform it?
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It leaks storage decisions into a contract you cannot change, so every future migration — re-sharding, key type changes, replacing a batch job with streaming — becomes a breaking API change. The contract inherits the change cost you were trying to contain.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Build serializers as whitelists that name each output field, never as spreads with fields deleted. Re-read predict-run snippet 2.B: a spread is a blacklist, and the next migration joins the public contract silently.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The API should return exactly what the screen needs — that's what makes the frontend fast.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It couples the least changeable layer to the most volatile one. Formatting, badge text and row structure become contract, and the second client — a widget, a partner, a redesign — cannot get the underlying facts back out.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For every field, ask: would this field still make sense if the screen were redesigned tomorrow? Formatted strings and colors always fail that test.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Nullability is a detail; we'll settle it once we see how the API gets used.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It is the single hardest property to change after release, because the change is asymmetric: tightening is safe but loosening breaks every consumer that dereferenced the field. Real usage is precisely what makes it unchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Default every uncertain field to nullable before v1 and tighten later. In JavaScript, verify with a key-presence test — `undefined` silently deletes the key from the serialized response.

competencies.title: Evolving an API without breaking consumers
competencies.description: Select and apply an evolution strategy — additive change, field deprecation, URI, media-type or header versioning — and define what makes a change breaking for a given consumer population.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify a set of changes as breaking or non-breaking for a named consumer population and choose a proportionate strategy for each.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names the consumer population explicitly and reaches for telemetry before versioning.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If we need a breaking change, we ship /v2.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Versioning is a distribution strategy, not a design one. It duplicates the entire surface area, doubles the code paths, and does not migrate anyone — it gives every consumer permission to move never, which means you run v1 forever.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Before proposing a version, try the cheaper ladder: additive field plus deprecation plus usage telemetry, then media-type negotiation. Reserve URI versioning for a genuine redesign of the resource model.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adding a field is always backward compatible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It holds only for lenient consumers. Strict schema validators reject unknown fields, payload-size-sensitive clients degrade, and any consumer that round-trips your response back to you now sends a field you must handle.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Publish the leniency rule — 'clients MUST ignore unknown fields' — as part of the contract on day one, so a strict consumer is out of compliance rather than you being out of options.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: GraphQL is versionless, so evolution is free.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: 'Versionless' is a statement about URL structure, not about evolution cost. Removing a field still breaks whoever selected it. What GraphQL actually gives you is field-level usage telemetry as a built-in — which makes deprecation cheap, and that is the real advantage.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Ask the same question in either paradigm: which consumers still read this field, and how would I know? If you cannot answer, you cannot deprecate.

competencies.title: Designing stable, bounded result sets
competencies.description: Choose and implement offset, keyset/cursor or hybrid pagination given sort stability, mutation rate, and whether total counts are genuinely required.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement keyset pagination over a totally-ordered sort key and demonstrate stability under concurrent writes.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Sort key is provably total; the cursor encodes boundary sort-key values, not a position; the total-count decision is argued from cost.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: OFFSET pagination is fine as long as you have the right index.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The engine still produces and discards every skipped row, so cost grows with page depth regardless of index. And the second failure — duplicates and skips under concurrent writes — is a correctness defect that no index and no hardware addresses.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run predict-run snippet 3.A and watch a row appear on two consecutive pages with a perfect index in place. Then state the cost of your endpoint as a function of page depth.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A cursor is just an encoded offset — base64 the page number and you have cursor pagination.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The encoding is cosmetics; the semantics are what matter. A real cursor encodes the sort-key values of the boundary row, which is what makes the query a range seek and makes results stable under concurrent insertion and deletion.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Decode your own cursor. If what comes out is a number that could be multiplied by page size, you have offset pagination wearing a costume.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Clients need a total count and page numbers.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Exact counts over large mutable filtered sets are frequently the most expensive part of the request and are wrong by the time they render. Page numbers are a paper-era convention that imposes offset semantics on your database whether or not any user needs them.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Ask what the user is trying to do. 'See recent items' is infinite scroll; 'find a specific item' is search. Neither needs a page number, and an approximate count from table statistics usually satisfies the badge.

competencies.title: Diagnosing and eliminating query amplification
competencies.description: Detect N+1 and related fan-out patterns from query logs or traces, and remedy them with joins, batching or dataloader-style coalescing while reasoning about the tradeoff each introduces.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict emitted query counts for a resolution path and choose join versus batch per relation, with the tradeoff stated.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Decides by counting emitted queries and transferred rows, not by rule of thumb; distinguishes parallelism from batching.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The ORM handles N+1 for you.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The ORM usually causes it: lazy loading resolves a relation on first access and is the default, while eager loading is opt-in and fragile — move a field access into a template during a refactor and the N+1 returns with no diff that looks like a performance change.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Add a query-count assertion to the test for any list endpoint. It is the only N+1 regression test that survives a faster machine.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: N+1 is an ORM problem, or a GraphQL problem.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It is a property of per-item resolution, full stop. A hand-written loop produces it identically, and a service call per item produces it at 20ms of network instead of 2ms of database — the same defect, an order of magnitude more expensive, and invisible to every database tool you own.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Count round trips at every boundary the request crosses, not just at the database. A trace that stops at your own process boundary hides the expensive half.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One big join always beats N queries.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Joins across a one-to-many relation multiply rows: fifty episodes joined to thirty chapters each returns fifteen hundred rows, repeating the full episode payload thirty times. You can move the bottleneck from round trips to transfer and client-side deduplication.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Join for many-to-one (adds columns, not rows); batch with a single IN query for one-to-many. Decide by counting transferred rows, not queries alone.

competencies.title: Analyzing downstream client constraints
competencies.description: Predict how a given API shape constrains the frontend — request waterfalls, cache granularity, loading and error states, optimistic updates — and redesign the contract to relax the binding constraint.

desiredOutcomes.description: Identify the binding constraint in a client-side performance problem and propose an additive contract change that relaxes it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names waterfall depth explicitly where it applies, and the proposed fix is additive for existing consumers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The frontend can compose whatever it needs from the endpoints we already have.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It can — at the cost of sequential dependent fetches, which are the dominant term in perceived latency on mobile. The composition happens either way; the only question is whether it happens once on your server or on every client, over the network, at the user's latency.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Count round trips as the client must actually make them, marking which stages cannot start until a previous stage returns. That number, not payload size, is usually the problem.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A backend-for-frontend is over-engineering at our size.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: When client needs genuinely diverge, the composition layer exists either way — the choice is only whether it sits on your server once or is re-implemented inside every client. Rejecting it on principle usually means paying for it several times.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Before rejecting a BFF, check the cheaper additive options first: an opt-in expansion parameter, or one composed endpoint. If client needs have genuinely diverged, price the re-implementation you are choosing instead.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Over-fetching is just a bandwidth problem.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It also dictates cache-invalidation scope. A coarse composed response is invalidated by a change to any of its inputs, so one changed field throws away everything; fine-grained resources cache independently and invalidate precisely.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For any composed endpoint, list its inputs and ask what happens to the cached response when each one changes. That list is the real cost of the coarse shape.

sections.title: Data Shape at Rest: Modeling for the Queries You Actually Run
sections.description: Derive storage model and schema from enumerated access patterns and required transaction boundaries, rather than from entity diagrams or vendor defaults. Teaching domain: **parcel logistics**.

learningObjectives.description: Given a workload profile, select relational or document storage and defend the choice against the two strongest counterarguments.
Translate a frequency-ranked list of queries into a concrete schema with keys, indexes and justified denormalizations.
Identify which invariants must hold atomically and place aggregate and transaction boundaries accordingly.
Predict the failure mode of a proposed schema when a stated access pattern doubles in frequency or a new one appears.

motivationHooks.prompt: You have inherited a schema that was correct on day one and hostile by month eighteen. The cost was never a slow query — it was that the fix required a migration, the migration required a window, the window required sign-off, so the team built a cache instead. Six months later the cache is the source of truth and nobody can state the invariants.

Here is a claim you will probably resist: **adding an index to the hot query can make it forty times faster and still leave the design broken.** Before you read on, write down one situation where that could be true.

The situation is any query whose answer lives in a second table. The index made *finding* the newest scan cheap per row; it did not remove the visit. Triple the traffic and you triple the visits — which is why the win evaporated and no amount of hardware brought it back.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

**Access patterns are design inputs, not profiling discoveries.** A schema is a plan for answering a specific ranked set of questions; you cannot evaluate a plan against an unstated goal.

**Indexes change the cost of selection; shape changes the cost of access.** If a request must visit a second structure, an index makes the visit fast without removing it.

**Duplication and staleness are independent.** A denormalized column written in the same transaction as the fact it summarizes, with an ordering guard, is never stale.

**Consistency is topology, not data model.** A single-node document store is strongly consistent; a relational replica is not.

**Boundaries are drawn around invariants.** Whatever crosses a boundary needs idempotency, compensation, or a smaller boundary — never a transaction that does not exist.
keyTakeaways: Rank the queries by frequency before drawing a single table.
An index cannot rescue a shape that forces a second visit per request.
A denormalized column is stale only if the write path made it so.
Name the access pattern you deliberately made slow — a design with no sacrifice made no decision.
Choosing a document model relocates the schema into your readers; name the version tag and the validator.

learningExperiences.title: Kestrel Freight: deriving a schema from the questions

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

Everything downstream in this course — the contract you publish in Section 2, the pagination and query amplification you pay for in Section 3 — is constrained by decisions made here.

You can change an API with a deprecation cycle. Changing the shape of ten billion rows is a project with a budget. That asymmetry is why this section comes first, and why it installs exactly one habit: **enumerate the access patterns before you draw a single table.**

### What you will be able to do

- Select relational or document storage from a workload profile, and defend it against the two strongest counterarguments.
- Turn a frequency-ranked list of queries into a schema with keys, indexes and justified denormalizations.
- Place transaction boundaries around invariants, and choose correctly when an invariant crosses one.
- Predict how a schema fails when an access pattern doubles or a new one appears.

contentBlocks.title: About the code in this course
contentBlocks.content: Code here runs in your browser. JavaScript works offline. **Python and SQL runtimes download once on first use, so the first run of a Python or SQL widget needs a network connection**; after that they are cached. Where this course uses test suites, the environment is a *Jest-compatible subset* — `describe`, `it`, `expect`, common matchers, `beforeEach`/`afterEach`, `jest.fn` — not Jest itself. No module mocking, snapshots or fake timers.

## A concrete failure

Kestrel Freight moves parcels between depots. Every time a parcel is handled, a handheld scanner emits a **scan event**: parcel ID, depot code, timestamp, handler.

The original model was the obvious one:

```
parcel(id, recipient_name, recipient_address, service_level, created_at)
scan(id, parcel_id, depot_code, scanned_at, handler_id)
```

That is a clean third-normal-form model, and by that standard it is correct. Now look at what the system is actually asked.

contentBlocks.caption: The access patterns nobody wrote down before drawing the tables
rows: Where is parcel X right now?
What is the full history of parcel X?
Which parcels are sitting at depot D, oldest first?
How many parcels did handler H scan yesterday?

contentBlocks.content:
Q1 is ninety-nine percent of the load, and in the clean model it has no cheap answer. "Where is it right now" means "the depot code of the scan row with the largest `scanned_at` for this parcel" — a sort or an aggregate over a group, per request, forty thousand times a minute.

You can index `scan(parcel_id, scanned_at DESC)` and it will help enormously. But notice precisely what the index did and did not do. It made *finding* the newest row fast. It did not remove the fact that answering a question about one parcel requires visiting a second table at all.

That distinction is the whole section.

contentBlocks.title: Misconception: "an index will fix it"
contentBlocks.content:
An index accelerates **selection** — finding the qualifying rows. It cannot change **shape** — how many structures a request must touch and whether a value is recomputed per request.

The diagnostic question is not "is this query slow?" but **"is the cost per row, or is it the number of visits?"** Only the first is an index problem. When p99 improves forty-fold and then degrades in proportion to traffic, you are looking at the second.

## The rewrite, derived from the access patterns

Start from the table of questions, not the nouns.

```
parcel(
  id, recipient_name, recipient_address, service_level, created_at,
  current_depot,       -- denormalized: answers Q1 with no join
  last_scanned_at,     -- denormalized
  scan_count           -- denormalized
)
scan(id, parcel_id, depot_code, scanned_at, handler_id)

INDEX parcel_depot_age  ON parcel(current_depot, last_scanned_at)  -- Q3
INDEX scan_parcel_time  ON scan(parcel_id, scanned_at DESC)        -- Q2
INDEX scan_handler_time ON scan(handler_id, scanned_at)            -- Q4
```

Q1 is now a single-row primary key lookup. Q3 is a range scan on one index, on one table. Q2 and Q4 are unchanged and were never hot.

The near-universal objection is that duplicated data drifts. It drifts only if you let it — so watch the write path.

terms.definition: A specific question the system must answer, stated with its frequency. The ranked set of access patterns is the design input a schema is an answer to.
Deliberately storing a fact in more than one place so a hot read needs fewer visits. Independent of staleness, which is a property of the write path.
The line drawn around facts that must never be observed half-applied. What crosses it needs idempotency, compensation, or a smaller boundary.
Applying the same message twice has the same effect as applying it once — the property that makes a retryable cross-service write safe.

contentBlocks.caption: Run it: the aggregate-per-request that an index makes fast but cannot remove.

contentBlocks.content:
### An analogy worth keeping

Think of an index as a good filing clerk and shape as the floor plan of the building.

A brilliant clerk finds any file in the archive room in seconds. But if answering a customer's question requires walking to the archive room at all — every time, for every customer — then hiring a faster clerk buys you a fixed multiple and nothing more. Triple the customers and you triple the walks.

Moving the one fact customers actually ask for onto the front desk is a floor-plan change. That is what a denormalized column is, and it is why the index and the summary column are not competing solutions to the same problem.

contentBlocks.caption: Scratch space: falsify it yourself. Change `hub <> 'SJC'` to `hub IS NOT 'SJC'`, or add more NULL rows, and see which rows survive the filter.

contentBlocks.content:
## When the boundary does not fit

Kestrel splits depot operations into its own service with its own database. A handoff now means: mark the parcel departed in the Logistics DB, **and** create an inbound expectation in the Depot DB.

The reflex is to wrap both in a transaction. There is no shared transaction manager across two services with two databases, so there is no transaction to open. The honest options are three:

1. **Collapse the boundary.** Put both facts back in one database. Unfashionable, frequently correct.
2. **Make the second write idempotent and retryable.** Emit `handoff(parcel=1, to=OAK, seq=17)`; the Depot service applies it and ignores replays of `seq=17`.
3. **Compensate.** Accept the window, detect divergence with reconciliation, emit a correcting action.

And ask the right question about the window. Not "how long is the gap?" but **"what does a customer see during the gap, and is that acceptable?"** Here the tracking page shows "departed SJC" with no arrival yet, which reads fine to a human — fortunate, because eventual consistency guarantees no bound at all. A design that is only correct when lag is small is a bet, not a design.

## Common errors in this material

- **"Normalize first, optimize later."** Treats the dominant access pattern as a tuning detail to be discovered after the shape is frozen — when the shape *is* the answer to it. The fix costs a migration on your largest table, which is the fix that never gets budget.
- **"An index will fix it."** Confuses selection cost with access shape. Diagnostic: does the improvement survive a tripling of traffic?
- **"Denormalized means stale."** Confuses duplication with asynchrony. If your copy is stale, the bug is in the write path.
- **"Relational is consistent, document is eventual."** Confuses data model with topology. Name the nodes before making a consistency claim.
- **"Wrap the two service calls in a transaction."** There is nothing to wrap. Pick one of the three real options instead.

contentBlocks.content:
## Section takeaway

Three rules, in order.

1. **Access patterns are design inputs.** Rank the questions by frequency before drawing tables.
2. **Indexes change selection cost; shape changes access cost.** If a query must visit a second structure, an index makes the visit fast but does not remove it.
3. **Draw transaction boundaries around invariants.** What must never be seen half-applied? That set defines the boundary; anything crossing it needs idempotency, compensation, or a smaller boundary.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before running this, predict all three result values. Most developers get the second and third wrong, and the reason they are wrong is a modeling decision, not a SQL trivia point.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
`NULL` is not a value meaning "none"; it is a marker meaning **unknown**. Comparing an unknown to anything yields `UNKNOWN`, and `WHERE` keeps only rows evaluating to `TRUE`, so parcel 2 is silently dropped from `hub <> 'SJC'`. The third query is the one that bites in production: the subquery returns the set `{'SJC', NULL}`, and `'OAK' NOT IN ('SJC', NULL)` expands to `NOT('OAK'='SJC' OR 'OAK'=NULL)` → `NOT(FALSE OR UNKNOWN)` → `UNKNOWN`. Every row is filtered out and the query returns zero rows with no error, no warning and no plan anomaly.

This is why nullability is a *modeling* decision rather than a column attribute — and it is the same reason it becomes a contract decision in Section 2.

codeExercise.explanation: The results are 3 and 2, then 1, then 0. The third is the dangerous one: a `NOT IN` against a subquery that can yield `NULL` returns nothing at all, silently. If you have ever seen a filter "work in staging and return nothing in production", this is very often why — production simply had a null the fixture did not.

interactionSequence.prompt: Your tracking endpoint answers "where is parcel X" by selecting the newest row from a four-billion-row `scan` table. You add `INDEX scan(parcel_id, scanned_at DESC)`; p99 drops from 400ms to 12ms. Traffic then triples and p99 returns to 180ms. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: The index removed the scan but not the per-request visit to a second table; under load, the remaining work still scales with request volume.
The index is the correct and complete fix; the real problem is insufficient hardware, so scale the read replicas.
The planner is no longer choosing the index; refresh statistics and add a query hint.
The table should be migrated to a document store, where this lookup is inherently faster.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct — the index changed selection cost, not access shape. Each request still performs a lookup in `scan` that a denormalized `current_depot` column would eliminate entirely.
No amount of hardware removes work the shape makes mandatory, and the symptom scaling with request count is the tell that this is per-request work.
Plausible ops instinct, but a plan regression appears suddenly rather than in proportion to traffic.
The speedup attributed to document stores comes from co-locating related data — which you can do relationally with a summary column, without changing engines.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Hold on to the diagnostic: **does the improvement survive a tripling of traffic?** Per-row costs do; per-request visits do not. This exact question returns in Section 3, where `OFFSET` pagination turns out to be the same distinction wearing different clothes.
hints: The improvement was real and then partly evaporated. What kind of cost behaves that way?
Write the cost as a function: cost = (requests) × (work per request). Which term did the index reduce?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this diagnosis?

interactionSequence.prompt: A reviewer objects to adding `parcel.current_depot` on the grounds that "denormalized data goes stale." What is the strongest correct response?
options: Staleness comes from writing the copy asynchronously, not from the copy existing; written in the same transaction as the scan, with an ordering guard, it cannot be stale.
Correct, but the staleness window will only be a few hundred milliseconds, which is acceptable for a tracking page.
Correct in principle, so we should normalize now and add the column later if profiling shows we need it.
It doesn't matter, because we'll put the current depot in a cache, which is the standard way to serve hot reads.

optionFeedback.feedback: Exactly. Duplication and staleness are independent properties, and the write path is what separates them.
This concedes an asynchronous write path unnecessarily, and assumes a bound on lag that nothing guarantees.
Deferring the shape decision turns it into a migration on a huge table — the dominant access pattern is a design input, not a profiling discovery.
A cache is a second copy written outside the transaction, which reintroduces exactly the staleness the reviewer feared, plus an invalidation problem.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Note how option 4 is the trap most teams actually fall into. Rejecting a denormalized column as "unsafe" and then adding a cache is choosing the *same* duplication with *worse* guarantees: outside the transaction, with an invalidation problem attached. If you are going to keep a second copy, keep it where the database can write it atomically.

interactionSequence.prompt: Put these five activities in the order a competent modeler performs them, best first.
options: Enumerate and rank the queries the system must answer, with frequencies
Identify which facts must never be observed half-applied
Choose tables or collections and their keys
Add indexes for the ranked access patterns
Run a profiler against production and tune what shows up hot

optionFeedback.feedback: First. Everything after it is an answer to a question this step poses.
Second. Invariants determine what must be co-located, so boundaries precede table choice.
Third. Keys and collections fall out once you know the questions and the invariants.
Fourth. An index is an accelerator for a shape that already exists — it cannot create one.
Last, and it is validation rather than design. Putting it first means discovering the dominant access pattern only after the shape is expensive to change.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The ordering that teams actually use is 3 → 4 → 5 → 1, with step 2 never happening at all. That sequence produces a schema that is defensible in review and hostile in production, because it was evaluated against a goal nobody stated.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this ordering?

interactionSequence.prompt:
Implement the guard that keeps a denormalized summary correct when scans arrive out of order.

`apply_scan(current_hub, last_at, incoming_hub, incoming_at)` returns the parcel's new summary as a two-element list `[hub, last_at]`. Scanners buffer when offline, so a 14:02 scan can arrive *after* a 14:40 scan — and a summary that moves backwards is **wrong**, not merely stale.

Only the marked region is editable. Iterate freely; you are expected to run Check more than once.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This four-line function is the entire refutation of "denormalized means stale". In the real schema it lives inside the `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` clause — `AND (last_scanned_at IS NULL OR last_scanned_at < :at)` — which matters because doing the check in application code lets two concurrent scans both read the old value and both decide to write. The predicate makes the check and the write one atomic operation.
hints: There are three situations, not two: a newer scan, an older scan, and the very first scan for a parcel.
What is `last_at` before any scan has ever been recorded? Comparing that value directly will not do what you want.
For two scans with identical timestamps, keep what you already have — a tie is not new information.

codeExercise.starterCode:
def apply_scan(current_hub, last_at, incoming_hub, incoming_at):
    """Return the parcel's new summary as [hub, last_at].

    Accept the incoming scan only when it is strictly newer than what
    we already have. `last_at` is None before the first scan.
    """
    # [[edit]]
    return [incoming_hub, incoming_at]
    # [[/edit]]
codeExercise.solutionNote:
In production this becomes a predicate rather than a branch:

```sql
UPDATE parcel
   SET current_depot = :hub, last_scanned_at = :at, scan_count = scan_count + 1
 WHERE id = :id
   AND (last_scanned_at IS NULL OR last_scanned_at < :at);
```

Same logic, but now the read and the write cannot be interleaved by a concurrent scan.

identical timestamps: keep what you have

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Practical activity — Kestrel Depot Dashboard.**

You are handed this access-pattern table for a new depot-floor tool:

| Pattern | Frequency | Latency budget |
|---|---|---|
| A1 parcels at my depot, oldest first, 50 at a time | 2,000/min | 100ms |
| A2 count of parcels at my depot by service level | 2,000/min (same screen) | 100ms |
| A3 full scan history for one parcel | 40/min | 800ms |
| A4 all parcels that missed their SLA yesterday | 1/day | 60s |

Write out four things:

1. A schema — tables, columns, indexes — with a one-line justification per index naming which pattern it serves.
2. Every denormalized column, and for each, the exact transaction in which it is maintained.
3. One sentence naming the invariant that defines your transaction boundary.
4. One sentence naming the pattern you have deliberately made slow, and why that is acceptable.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Deliverable 4 is the graded one. **A design with no deliberate sacrifice has not made a decision.**

A strong answer sacrifices A4 — a once-a-day query with a sixty-second budget has no claim on your shape. It will run as a filtered scan over `scan` joined to `parcel` and that is entirely fine.

A2 is the subtle one. It looks like it needs an aggregate per request at 2,000/min, which is the Q1 problem again. Two honest treatments: maintain per-depot per-service counters transactionally (the same pattern as `scan_count`), or accept the aggregate because the filtered set per depot is small and bounded. Either is defensible; *not noticing that A2 is an aggregate on the hot path* is not.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words, and without reusing the parcel example: explain to a colleague the difference between what an index changes and what schema shape changes. Then name one query in a system you have actually worked on where an index could not have rescued the design.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The test of whether this landed is whether your example involves a **second visit** or a **per-request recomputation**. Common real ones: an unread-count badge computed by counting rows per user on every page load; a "latest status" derived from an event log; a permission check that walks a hierarchy per request. All three are shape problems wearing index-shaped clothing.

workedExamples.title: The write path that makes denormalization safe
workedExamples.problem: A scanner reports: parcel 1 handled at depot OAK at 14:02. The `parcel` table carries denormalized `current_depot`, `last_scanned_at` and `scan_count`. Write the update so that the summary is never wrong — including when scans arrive out of order.
steps: **Identify what must be true after the write.** Two facts must hold together: the scan is in the log, *and* `parcel.current_depot` reflects the newest scan. If one lands without the other, the tracking page lies.

**Decide whether both facts live inside one transaction boundary.** Both live in the same database, so the boundary can contain both. There is no distributed problem to solve here — recognising that is half the work, because teams routinely reach for messaging when a transaction was available.

**Notice the guard clause.** The `AND last_scanned_at < ...` predicate handles out-of-order arrival. Scanners buffer when offline, so a 14:02 scan can arrive after a 14:40 scan. Without the guard the denormalized column would be *wrong*, not stale — a different and worse failure.
**Check the null branch.** `last_scanned_at IS NULL` must be there, or the very first scan for a parcel never lands, because `NULL < anything` is `UNKNOWN` rather than `TRUE`.
workedExamples.conclusion: **`parcel.current_depot` is never stale, because it is never written outside the transaction that creates the fact it summarizes.** Duplication and staleness are independent properties: duplication written asynchronously is stale, duplication written transactionally is just a second physical copy of a fact that was committed once. If a denormalized column in your system *is* stale, the defect is in the write path — not in the decision to denormalize.

fadedVariant.problem: Kestrel adds a `depot` table with a denormalized `parcels_on_hand` counter, so the depot dashboard can show occupancy without an aggregate. A parcel is transferred from SJC to OAK, and both counters must move. Complete the missing steps.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Identify what must be true after the write.** Three facts: the scan is logged, SJC's counter has decreased by one, and OAK's counter has increased by one.

**Step 3 — Write the statements.** One `INSERT` into `scan`, one `UPDATE depot ... SET parcels_on_hand = parcels_on_hand - 1 WHERE code = 'SJC'`, one `UPDATE depot ... + 1 WHERE code = 'OAK'`, plus the guarded `UPDATE parcel`.
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2 — Where does the transaction boundary go, and what is the invariant that defines it?
Step 4 — What goes wrong if the two depot counter updates are applied in a different order by two concurrent transfers, and what stops it?
Step 5 — The counters are derived data. State the one-sentence rule that tells you they will not drift.
blankedStepAnswers: The boundary encloses all four statements, in one transaction in one database. The invariant is that the sum of `parcels_on_hand` across depots equals the number of parcels currently held — it must never be observed half-applied, or the dashboard shows a parcel in two places or nowhere.

Two concurrent transfers touching the same pair of depots in opposite orders can deadlock. The fix is to acquire the depot rows in a deterministic order — for example, always update the lower depot code first — or to express both updates as a single statement over both rows. Note this is a concurrency concern, not a correctness-of-denormalization concern.
They will not drift because every change to a counter happens inside the same transaction as the scan that causes it, and never anywhere else — there is exactly one write path to the derived value.

workedExamples.title: Relational or document? Deriving the answer from the workload
workedExamples.problem: Kestrel wants to store the **scan payload** — whatever the handheld device attached. Barcode-only devices send three fields. New camera units send a photo hash, GPS fix, temperature, and a nested list of damage markers. Vendors add fields quarterly, without asking. Choose a storage model.
steps: **Write down the access patterns for this data specifically.** P1: show everything attached to scan S (whole-document read, by key, high volume). P2: find scans where temperature exceeded 8°C (query across a payload field, ~10/day, cold-chain audits). There is no P3 — nobody joins on payload fields, nobody aggregates them in real time.
**Characterize the write side.** Writes are append-only. A payload is never partially updated. Schema churn is quarterly and driven by an external party you do not control.

**Evaluate the cost of change under each model.** Relational columns: every vendor field addition is a migration on a very large table — a cost the access patterns do not justify, since P1 does not need columns and P2 runs ten times a day. Document/JSON: whole-document read by key is the native operation, and P2 is a slow scan, acceptable at ten a day and accelerable later with an expression index.

**Ask where the schema went.** This is the step people skip. Choosing a document representation did not abolish the schema; it moved enforcement out of the database and into every reader. So the model is incomplete until you name the owner: a `payload_version` field written with every document, plus a validating parser at the read boundary. That *is* the schema, and it now lives in code and must be versioned like code.

**Check what did not enter the decision.** Speed did not. A document store is not inherently faster; where it appears faster the cause is co-located access, and co-locating the same data relationally produces the same win.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Store the payload as a document, with an explicit `payload_version` and a validating reader; keep `parcel` and `scan` relational.** The relational tables carry the invariants — a scan belongs to exactly one parcel, and `current_depot` must agree with the newest scan — and invariants are exactly what a relational engine enforces for free. Note too what a JSONB column would and would not settle: it gives flexible fields inside a transactional engine, which is often right, but it does not change transaction scope, give the planner statistics on nested values, or answer who validates the payload. The tradeoff moves; it does not vanish.

transferExercises.scenario: A geological survey runs 8,000 ground sensors. Each emits a reading every second: timestamp, station ID, three axis values. Two questions dominate: **(a)** a public map showing every station's *current* reading, refreshed every 5 seconds; **(b)** researchers pulling one station's full waveform for a date range, a few dozen times a day. Readings are never updated after write.
transferExercises.task: Produce the storage model choice with justification, the schema, the denormalized columns and the transaction in which each is maintained, and the one access pattern you are deliberately making slow.

Pattern (b) is served by an index on `(station_id, timestamp)` and is explicitly identified as the pattern you are *not* optimizing beyond that.
The justification argues from access patterns and cost of change, never from 'time-series databases are faster'.
The append-only write pattern is used as evidence in the reasoning, not merely mentioned.
You name what an observer sees if the current-reading update and the reading insert were ever split across a boundary.

The ward stock system is a separate service with its own database. Regulation requires that the count never be understated, and that no administration is ever lost.

Chooses among collapse / idempotent message / compensate, with a reason tied to the regulatory constraint rather than to fashion.
Describes what an auditor sees *during* the window in concrete terms, not how long the window lasts.
Addresses the asymmetry in the requirement: understating the count is prohibited, which points toward decrementing first or reserving.

learningExperiences.title: Field exercise: audit a schema you own

contentBlocks.content: The rules in this section are cheap to agree with and expensive to apply. This exercise makes you apply them once, to a schema you are actually responsible for, before the ideas fade.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Produce a one-page access-pattern audit of a table you own, ending in a single named design decision you would change.

instructions: Pick the single busiest table in a system you maintain. Busiest by *read volume*, not row count.

sections.title: Data Shape on the Wire: Contracts That Survive Change
sections.description: Design the API as an independent model with its own paradigm, semantics and evolution strategy, deliberately decoupled from both the schema beneath and the screens above. Teaching domain: **municipal transit ticketing**.

learningObjectives.description: Given client diversity, caching needs and team topology, select REST, GraphQL or RPC and state the specific costs the choice incurs.
Design a resource contract that does not mirror the storage schema, and articulate each place it deliberately diverges.
Specify nullability, identifier and error semantics, and justify each as a decision that is expensive to reverse.
Classify proposed changes as breaking or non-breaking for a defined consumer population and select an evolution strategy for each.
Critique a contract that leaks storage or UI structure, and refactor it to remove the leak.

motivationHooks.prompt: A schema is a decision you can reverse with a migration and a maintenance window. A published contract is a decision you can reverse only with the cooperation of every consumer — some of them mobile apps on devices that will never be updated, some of them partners who will not answer your email.

Predict before reading: of the two obvious ways to design a response body — mirror the database table, or mirror the screen — **which one is the more dangerous mistake, and why?** Commit to an answer now.

Both wrong answers are locally efficient. Exposing the tables is the fastest way to ship. Matching the screens is the fastest way to make the frontend happy this sprint. Both trade a week now for a multi-year constraint.

The honest answer is that they are dangerous in different directions, and the choice between them is a false one. Exposing tables binds your contract to the layer with the *highest change cost below it*; matching screens binds it to the layer with the *highest change rate above it*. The contract is a third model, and a v1 shaped by either neighbour is already a constraint you will be paying for in two years.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

**The contract is a third model.** Derive it from domain facts and consumer lifetimes, not from tables below or screens above.

**Loosening is breaking; tightening is safe.** Default every uncertain field to the loose end and tighten once you are sure — you will never get to loosen later.

**"Breaking" is undefined without a consumer population.** Write the population down first, including the strict validators and the clients you cannot update.

**Paradigm choice is per audience.** Composition, caching, cost-bounding and updatability are the axes; there is no global winner, and mature systems run both.

**Telemetry precedes versioning.** You cannot deprecate what you cannot measure, and `/v2` without usage data postpones the migration rather than performing it.
keyTakeaways: Opaque string identifiers are the cheapest insurance in contract design.
Money is always an object with a currency, from v1.
Nullability is settled before first release, because it cannot be loosened afterwards.
A serializer must be a whitelist that names its outputs, never a spread with fields deleted.
Publish 'clients MUST ignore unknown fields' on day one, so strict consumers are out of compliance rather than you being out of options.

learningExperiences.title: Meridian Transit: the contract as its own model

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

Senior developers know in the abstract that the API is not the database, and violate it in practice, because both wrong answers are locally efficient.

By the end of this experience you will be able to look at a proposed response body and say which parts are storage leaking out, which parts are UI leaking in, and which single field is going to make the next migration a breaking change.

**Carried forward from Section 1:** you already know that an index cannot change shape. The same asymmetry applies here in a harsher form — a contract has no equivalent of a migration window.

## A concrete leak

Meridian Transit runs buses and light rail. Their storage model, designed well by Section 1's rules, looks like this:

```
tap(id, rider_id, station_id, tapped_at, fare_cents, internal_cost_cents,
    settlement_batch_id, void_reason, fare_rule_version)
```

The first version of the rider-facing API was generated from this table:

```json
{ "id": 90214, "rider_id": 7, "station_id": 31,
  "tapped_at": "2026-09-19T14:02:11Z",
  "fare_cents": 275, "internal_cost_cents": 190,
  "settlement_batch_id": 4471, "void_reason": null,
  "fare_rule_version": 12 }
```

Count the problems before reading on.

**It publishes information that isn't the rider's business.** `internal_cost_cents` is now, effectively, disclosed operating-cost data. A journalist will find it.

**It publishes internal identifiers as integers.** `id: 90214` tells anyone watching how many taps Meridian has processed and — worse — commits you forever to integers. When taps move to a sharded store with composite keys, the type changes, and a type change is breaking.

**It publishes the storage model's *decisions*, not the domain's facts.** `settlement_batch_id` exists because of how the nightly job is structured. Replace the nightly job with streaming settlement and the field becomes meaningless — but it is in a contract, so it must keep being populated with something.

**It publishes `fare_cents` as a bare integer.** No currency. Meridian runs one currency today and will run a cross-border service in three years.

Every one of these is the same error: the contract was derived from the table.

contentBlocks.title: The correction that is also a trap
contentBlocks.content:
The obvious fix is to ask the frontend what it needs. They are building a trip-history screen, so:

```json
{ "rows": [ { "label": "Civic Center · 2:02 PM", "amountText": "$2.75",
              "badge": "CAPPED", "badgeColor": "#2b7" } ] }
```

This ships beautifully. Formatting (`"2:02 PM"`, `"$2.75"`), presentation (`badgeColor`) and screen structure (`rows`) are now contract. The screen is the most volatile layer you own — it will be redesigned twice before the API's first birthday — and you have bound the *least* changeable layer to the *most* changeable one. When the Android team ships a widget needing the raw timestamp, it cannot have it.

## The contract as its own model

The contract describes **domain facts, at a granularity the domain justifies, in representations chosen for longevity.**

```json
{ "id": "tap_9f3a21c0",
  "riderId": "rdr_7c19",
  "station": { "id": "stn_civic_center", "name": "Civic Center" },
  "occurredAt": "2026-09-19T14:02:11Z",
  "fare": { "amount": 275, "currency": "USD", "capped": true },
  "status": "settled",
  "voidReason": null }
```

Four deliberate choices, each with a reason:

- **Opaque string identifiers.** `tap_9f3a21c0` is a string forever, whatever the storage key becomes. This is the cheapest insurance policy in contract design, and a direct payoff from Section 1: you may need to re-shard or move to document storage, and that decision stays invisible.
- **Money as an object.** Adding a currency later means changing a number into an object, which is breaking. Starting with the object costs nothing.
- **A status enum, not internal state.** `"settled"` is a domain fact; `settlement_batch_id: 4471` was an implementation detail. If settlement becomes streaming, `"settled"` still means what it always meant.
- **Explicit null, deliberately.** `voidReason` is always present, sometimes null — which brings us to the field that will hurt you most.

### An analogy worth keeping

The contract is the printed menu. The storage schema is the kitchen's inventory system; the screen is the specials board by the door.

Print the inventory codes on the menu and you cannot change suppliers without reprinting. Print today's specials on it and you reprint every week. The menu has to name dishes — things a diner can order and a kitchen can make — which is neither of its neighbours.

And here is the part that makes a menu different from a whiteboard: once it is printed and handed out, you cannot recall the copies people took home. That is the whole reason this section's rules are stricter than Section 1's. A schema is a whiteboard. A published contract is in someone's coat pocket.

The written-down set of clients a contract serves, including their update cadence and leniency. Without it, 'breaking' is undefined.
A change that adds to a contract without removing, retyping or loosening anything existing — the cheapest rung of the evolution ladder.
Marking a field as going away, instrumenting who still reads it, and removing it only when that number reaches zero. Requires telemetry to complete.

contentBlocks.title: Misconception: "nullability is a detail for later"
contentBlocks.content:
Work the asymmetry in both directions.

**Non-nullable → nullable** ("this field can now be absent") breaks every consumer that dereferenced it without a check — a compile error at best, a null-pointer crash at worst. **Breaking.**

**Nullable → non-nullable** ("this field is now always present") leaves the consumer's existing null branch as dead code. **Non-breaking.**

You can always tighten. You can never loosen. So the default for any field whose future is uncertain is *nullable*, settled **before** first release — because real usage is exactly what makes it unchangeable.

Type change. Anything typed, sorted numerically, or used as a numeric key fails.
Loosening. Every consumer that dereferenced it now faces null.
Removal by another name, even if the key remains present with a null.

contentBlocks.content:
## The evolution ladder

The reflex for a genuinely breaking change is `/v2`. Understand what that buys: it duplicates the entire surface area, doubles the code paths, and does not migrate anyone. Every consumer still has to do the work; you have given them permission to do it never, which means you run v1 forever. **Versioning is a distribution strategy, not a design one.**

In order of preference:

1. **Additive plus deprecation.** Add `idString` beside `id`, mark `id` deprecated, instrument which consumers still read it, remove when the number reaches zero.
2. **Media-type or header negotiation.** `Accept: application/vnd.meridian.tap+json;v=2` — one URL, per-representation evolution, consumers opt in individually.
3. **URI versioning (`/v2/taps`).** Reserve for a genuine redesign where the resource *model* changed, not for a field type.

Reach for versioning last. Reach for telemetry first — you cannot deprecate what you cannot measure.

And for the GraphQL half of a system: "versionless" is a statement about URL structure, not evolution cost. Removing a field still breaks whoever selected it. What GraphQL actually gives you is field-level usage telemetry as a built-in, which makes step 1 cheap. *That* is the advantage, not the absence of versions.

## Common errors in this material

- **"The API should expose the tables."** Inherits the storage layer's change cost into a contract you cannot migrate.
- **"The API should match the screens."** Binds the least changeable layer to the most volatile one.
- **"Nullability is a detail to settle later."** It is the one property that cannot be loosened after release.
- **"Adding a field is always safe."** True for lenient consumers only. Publish the leniency rule instead of relying on it.
- **"Ship /v2."** Duplicates the surface and migrates nobody.
- **"GraphQL is versionless, so evolution is free."** It relocates the cost into needing field-level usage data — which, to be fair, it gives you.
- **"REST means JSON with the right verbs."** Identity, representation and cache semantics are the substance; verbs are the syntax.

contentBlocks.content:
## Section takeaway

- The contract is a third model, derived from domain facts and consumer lifetimes.
- Loosening is breaking; tightening is safe. Default loose, tighten when certain.
- "Breaking" is relative to a consumer population you must write down.
- Paradigm choice is per audience; caching, composition, cost-bounding and updatability are the axes.
- Telemetry precedes versioning, always.

interactionSequence.prompt: Predict all three lines of output exactly, including which keys survive. This one silently rewrites your contract, and the difference is invisible in code review.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Developers treat `null` and `undefined` as two spellings of "no value", and most JavaScript lets them get away with it. `JSON.stringify` does not: an `undefined` **object property is deleted entirely**, while an `undefined` **array element becomes `null`**, because arrays must preserve length.

So a serializer returning `undefined` for a missing nickname publishes "field absent", while one returning `null` publishes "field present and null" — and a single endpoint can emit both shapes depending on which code path ran. A strict client consuming both will reject half your traffic.

The third line adds two more silent conversions: `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`, and `Date` becomes an ISO string via `toJSON`. Part of your contract's types are being decided by `JSON.stringify` rather than by you.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team proposes a response body whose fields are exactly the columns of the backing table, renamed to camelCase. What is the primary risk?
options: Every future storage change — re-sharding, key type changes, replacing a nightly batch with streaming — becomes a breaking API change.
It's acceptable as a v1; you can reshape the contract later once real consumer needs are known.
The response will over-fetch, wasting bandwidth on mobile clients.
camelCase conversion is lossy and will cause collisions between similarly named columns.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. The contract has inherited the storage model's change cost, which is the one cost you were trying to keep on your side of the boundary.
'Reshape later' is exactly what a published contract makes expensive — consumers you don't control turn this into a permanent constraint.
Bandwidth is the least of it; the binding problem is coupling two models with very different change costs.
A real if minor naming concern, not the structural problem — the risk would be identical with snake_case preserved.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Connect this to Section 1. You spent that section learning to choose storage shape freely, driven by access patterns. Exposing the tables gives that freedom away: every future shape decision now has to clear a consumer-migration bar.

interactionSequence.prompt: You add a new nullable field `fare.discountReason` to an existing response. The consumer population includes an ETL job that validates payloads strictly and fails its nightly load on any unknown field. Classification?
options: Breaking for that consumer; the durable fix is to publish a 'clients MUST ignore unknown fields' rule as part of the contract.
Non-breaking; adding a field is backward compatible by definition.
Breaking, therefore you must ship /v2 with the new field and leave /v1 unchanged.
Non-breaking if you're on GraphQL, since GraphQL is versionless and additive changes are free there.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct on both halves: classification depends on the named population, and the mitigation is a contract rule rather than a restriction on your own ability to add fields.
This holds only for lenient consumers — strict validators, size-sensitive clients, and anything that echoes your payload back all falsify it.
Correct classification, wrong remedy: versioning the entire surface for one additive field duplicates everything and migrates no one.
'Versionless' describes URL structure, not evolution cost — a strict consumer is a strict consumer regardless of paradigm.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The important move here is that the leniency rule must exist **before** v1 ships. Published on day one, a strict consumer is out of compliance. Published in year three, you are the one who changed the deal.

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these responses to a needed breaking change, best (try first) to worst (last resort).
options: Add the new field alongside the old one, deprecate the old one, and instrument per-consumer usage until it reaches zero
Negotiate the representation per request via media type or version header on the same URL
Publish /v2 of the entire resource surface and run both indefinitely
Change the field in place and notify consumers by email
Change the field in place without notice, on the grounds that the contract never promised otherwise

optionFeedback.feedback: First. It lets consumers migrate individually, needs no new routing, and — crucially — lets you measure completion.
Second. Same individual opt-in as the first option, at the cost of negotiation machinery.
Third. It works, but duplicates the whole surface and postpones rather than performs the migration.
Fourth. Notice gives consumers a chance to react, but email is not a migration plan.
Last. Breaks consumers with no warning and no measurement.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Note that options 1 and 2 are the only two that produce **telemetry**. That is what actually separates them from `/v2`: not elegance, but the ability to know when you are finished.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Implement `toTapResource(row)` to emit exactly the published contract.

```
id:         "tap_<row.id>"
riderId:    "rdr_<row.rider_id>"
fare:       { amount: <row.fare_cents>, currency: "USD" }
status:     "void" when row.void_reason is non-null, else "valid"
voidReason: string | null — ALWAYS present as a key
internal_cost_cents: MUST NOT appear
```

Only the marked region is editable. Watch the free-transfer case.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The zero-fare case is the one most people fail, and it is not a JavaScript trivia point — it is the same error as SQL `NULL` semantics from Section 1. `if (row.fare_cents)` treats *absence* and *zero* as the same thing, and in a fare system they could hardly be more different.

Build the object by naming each output field. A spread plus `delete` looks like filtering and behaves like a blacklist: the next migration adds a column and it joins the public contract with no code change and no review.
hints: What does `if (row.fare_cents)` do when the fare is a free transfer?
One of the tests checks key *presence*, not value. What does `JSON.stringify` do to a key whose value is `undefined`?
Name each output field explicitly. Do not spread the input and remove fields from it.

codeExercise.solutionNote: Note the normalisation of `undefined` to `null` on the first line. Without it, a row missing `void_reason` entirely produces a response with no `voidReason` key at all — two contract shapes from one endpoint, invisible until a strict consumer rejects half your traffic.
